newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda stands to profit from Zaire occupation.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda stands to profit from Zaire occupation.

text.p: War-torn Rwanda's aid-addicted economy is likely to reap significant benefit from the capture of eastern Zaire by rebels it has favoured, according to analysts.
"I am very optimistic that as Rwanda integrates further with eastern Zaire it will bring great benefits for both countries," said Prosper Musafiri, a macroeconomist in the planning ministry.

Rebels fighting to overthrow Zaire's president of 31 years, Mobutu Sese Seko, now occupy a 1,000 km (625 miles) strip along the border with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi and have penetrated deep into the massive country at the heart of Africa.
Stirred by Zaire's decision to expel ethnic Tutsis, rebels made their initial advance into Zaire's Kivu region with vital assistance from Rwanda's Tutsi-led army.
"Kivu can become a bread basket for this country," Omar Bakhet, Kigali representative of the United Nations Development Programme told Reuters.

"With Kivu now not having the possibility to export to the other parts of Zaire it will naturally drift towards Rwanda. It is agriculturally very rich, minerally very rich and can have a big impact for this country even in the short term," he said.
Like Rwanda, East Zaire produces coffee and tea and has vast reserves of gold and other minerals. Previously it exported meat, fresh vegetables and tobacco to the rest of the country.

But the issue of regional integration is highly charged and Kinshasa has already accused Rwanda and its Ugandan allies of planning to annex territory and create a "Tutsiland" spanning Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and East Zaire.

Analysts say tiny, overpopulated Rwanda could not achieve economic self-sufficiency even with the greatest efforts to stimulate the main exports of coffee and tea. Subsistence agriculture dominates the economy, with tiny plots covering the steepest hillside.
Reserves of natural gas, discovered under Lake Kivu which borders the two countries, are so far untapped.
"There is always going to be growth when a country emerges from war and Rwanda has been helped by the return of the diaspora...but there is a limit to how far Rwanda can go," said Bakhet.
For years the biggest export has been human misery. An estimated 800,000 Tutsis were slaughtered in 1994 along with moderate Hutus in a genocide planned by members of the former Hutu government.
While coffee brought in an estimated $41 million in 1996 international development and emergency aid is put as high as $340 million in official figures.
Rwanda was reliant on aid and borrowed money even before the 1994 genocide and the flight into exile of two million refugees who feared reprisals for the genocide.

Over a million Hutu refugees returned at the end of last year after camps in eastern Zaire were overrun by the rebels. One consequence has been more instability as the Tutsi-dominated army battles Hutu militants who returned among the refugees.
But military sources say the cost of security will decline because many from the former Hutu-led army and militia have been driven deeper into Zaire and pose less of a threat.
There is no immediate prospect of paying off around a billion dollars in overseas debt, much incurred by the previous government as defence spending.

Rwanda's GDP growth stood at 25 percent in 1995 up from -50 percent the previous year, while inflation stood at 22.0 percent in 1995 up from 12.4 percent in 1993, according to World Bank figures. There was no 1994 inflation figure.
